text: TET-42: what a committed tetel artifact carries, with respect to machine-local absolute paths

All observations behind this memo were taken against a clean checkout of the tetel worktree on branch `main` at commit `01b140c74882b17ccb157839cf205794a0aaaa49`. Line numbers, counts and file contents cited below are that tree's; a reader checking them against a different commit should expect drift.
## The defect, restated from the artifacts

`render_facts` in `src/compose.rs` documents a contract under the heading "What is deliberately not here": the key is absolute, the label is repo-relative, only the label is rendered, and therefore "a committed document should not carry `/Users/<someone>/...`". Every clause of that sentence is a promise about committed artifacts, and the artifacts refute it. Three committed memos carry 218, 127 and 145 occurrences of a `/Users/` or `/Volumes/` path in their rendered markdown, and 448, 275 and 350 in the snapshot directories beside them. The comment is not describing a mechanism that exists; the same function's body builds the Extent column by mapping each extent entry to `e.label.as_str()`, printing whatever label was stored. TET-42 is therefore first a documentation defect and second a design question, and the two must be settled together — writing a true comment requires deciding what the true contract is.
## Where the path enters, and the one seam that can move

An extent entry carries two spellings of the same observation and they have different jobs. The key is `fs::canonicalize`d and used for machine comparison; the label is the path exactly as the caller spelled it, plus a line-range suffix, and is what a human reads. `mint` copies both across from the pending buffer field by field and computes neither, so the only place a label can be made repo-relative is where it is first written, in `observe.rs` — and the anchor such a rewrite would need is already sitting on the same pending entry, because `world_root` is resolved from the observed path at capture time.

The key cannot follow the label. `ExtentEntry::censuses`, the predicate every `target` declaration is checked against, asks `self.key == self.world_root`; `search_key` exists only to make those two tool-captured spellings of one absolute directory agree. Relativize the key and every census, and the overlap detection that shares the key, stops working. Whatever this design does, it does to labels alone.

That seam has a price attached, and it is worth naming before the decision rather than after. The pin is a sha256 over each entry's label, world_root, world_state and output — the key is not in it. So a capture-time label change is by construction a pin change: the same file, opened the same way at the same tree state, pins differently under the new build. Whether that costs anything depends on whether anything recomputes or cross-compares pins, which is settled below rather than assumed.

The pin discontinuity turns out to be cheap, and it is worth saying exactly how cheap, because "nothing uses it" is the kind of claim that ages badly. A sweep of every `.rs` file in `src/` and `tests/` for the word finds one computation site — the `sha256_hex` in `mint` — and no second one. `evidence.rs` copies a fact's pin into a recorded evidence statement; `query.rs` prints it; nothing anywhere recomputes it or compares two of them. The only tests that touch a fact pin assert that two pins minted in the same run are equal, and that two taken against different tree states are not; neither hard-codes a pin value, and both drive the CLI with a relative path. So a capture-time label change moves every future pin and breaks nothing. What it does not do is retroactively change a pin already on disk: pins are immutable per fact, so old facts keep old pins and new facts get new ones, and the two are never compared.

One naming hazard for whoever implements this: "pin" means two unrelated things here. A fact's pin is the content fingerprint discussed above. A memo's `pin:` is the commit hash an author writes into an evidence-ledger row or into a document-level "at pin `<hash>`" sentence, parsed by `ledger.rs` and `parse.rs`. Only the first moves.
## How this composes with TET-43

TET-43 is the standing observation that any change to render output reddens every committed memo. The mechanism is `snapshot::check`: it re-renders the snapshot in full and compares the result to the memo's committed bytes, so one changed character anywhere in the render path drifts all of them simultaneously. That is what makes the capture-time/render-time choice the load-bearing one in this design rather than a matter of taste. `render_facts` prints each stored label verbatim; it derives nothing. So a build that changes how labels are *captured* leaves every existing snapshot re-rendering byte-identically, and TET-43 never fires. A build that changes how labels are *rendered* detonates TET-43 by construction, for every memo, on the commit that lands it. This design takes the capture-time route, and its principal justification is that it does not require TET-43 to be solved first.

That gives the implementer an acceptance test with a number in it, and the number is not the one a prior investigation reported. This repository holds exactly eight committed rendered memos with snapshots, all under `docs/design/`, and on the build in the tree today every one of them checks at exit 0 with no `provenance-drift` line — verified against a deliberately corrupted copy, so the probe is known to fire. The baseline is 0 of 8, not 3 of 12. The acceptance condition for landing TET-42 is therefore the strict one: all eight must still be clean, with no drift attributable to this change and no pre-existing failure to hide behind.
## What the change buys, and what it cannot reach

The case for doing anything at all rests on one measurement: between 77% and 90% of the absolute paths in a committed memo point inside the repository the memo itself ships in. That is what separates this from cosmetics. A path rewritten from `/Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel/src/facts.rs` to `src/facts.rs` is not merely shorter; it is openable by the next reader who clones the repository, which the absolute form is not. The remaining 10-23% are paths to things outside the worktree, and nothing here can help them.

The same measurement bounds what the contract may promise, and this is where the ticket's own defect is easiest to repeat. Almost every absolute path in a rendered memo is a tool-generated extent label — but not all of them. Of the three memos measured, 0, 1 and 4 occurrences sit outside the Facts table, and those are of two kinds. Some are extent labels reaching the page through a second render site, the transplants section's "Donor extent (captured)" line at `src/compose.rs:195`, which the false doc comment at `src/compose.rs:252` does not even mention when it says "only the label is rendered". Others are author-typed claim propositions: tet56's C1 opens "The tree this memo's observations were taken against is `/Volumes/SSD/…`", and no label mechanism will ever touch it, because an author wrote it as prose. A contract promising "no machine-local path in a committed document" would therefore assert more than the mechanism can deliver — which is exactly the failure TET-42 exists to fix. The contract below is scoped to tool-generated citations for that reason.

Before the contract, one point about who is at fault, because it decides whether this is a documentation fix or a code change. An absolute label is not carelessness. The label is the path as the caller spelled it, and the MCP server through which every agent authors documents that every path-taking parameter must be absolute — a relative one resolves against a server working directory the caller cannot see or set, which has already cost one run its results. So an author who wanted a relative label could not produce one. The false comment describes a mechanism nobody built, and no amount of authoring discipline would have made it true.

One class of observation is exempt for a reason that has nothing to do with cost. A `run` records a command line, not a path: its key *is* the argv, and its label is `proc: {cmdline} (exit {exit_code})`. Rewriting any part of that would make the record assert that a command was run which was not run — trading a portability improvement for a falsified record of what executed. `proc:` labels stay verbatim, and a committed memo will keep carrying whatever absolute paths an author put on a command line.
## The anchor: `world_root`, not the memo's directory

Relative to what? Two candidates deserve the question. The memo's own directory matches the distribution unit a reader actually clones, which is an honest argument for it. It loses on availability: a capture-time mechanism runs before `render --out` has been called, so the memo has no location yet to be relative to. `world_root` — the observation's own `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` — is already on the pending entry at the moment the label is built, resolved from the observed path rather than from any process's working directory. And the two choices do not currently diverge: across all eight committed snapshots, every extent entry's world_root is either this repository or the degraded `no-git-worktree` marker. No committed memo cites a fact taken against a repository other than the one it ships in, so anchoring at the worktree root and anchoring at the memo's repository are the same anchor for the entire corpus. `world_root` wins on availability and costs nothing on the evidence available.

That choice comes with a gap the design must own rather than paper over. `src/facts.rs` is only openable if the reader knows which tree it is relative to, and a rendered memo does not say. `check` emits no row naming a memo's world root; the root survives in the snapshot's `facts.jsonl` and, by convention, in the author-typed pin claim that opens every memo in this corpus — but neither is a mechanism the tool enforces. Making the memo state its root would be a render change and is therefore TET-43's, not this ticket's. Until then the convention is load-bearing, and this memo names it as a precondition rather than pretending the relative label is self-describing.
## The forgery surface, and why the key is the input

The obvious implementation — strip the repo root off the front of the label — is unsound, and it is worth showing the attack rather than asserting it. Run on the current build: a `look` through a symlink that leaves the repository stores a label reading `<repo>/link/x.txt`, and a `look` spelled `<repo>/../outside/x.txt` stores that. Both labels textually begin with the repository root while naming a file outside it. A prefix strip would turn them into `link/x.txt` and `../outside/x.txt`, the first of which is a relative-looking citation to a file no reader of that repository has. In every one of those cases the key — canonicalized at capture — is the outside path, and the entry's own `world_root` is either `no-git-worktree` or the outside file's own repository, never the one the label appears to sit under.

That asymmetry is the design. The relative label is computed from the canonicalized key against the entry's own `world_root`, never by editing the string the caller typed. Under that rule the escape cases refuse themselves: the key is not under the repository root, so no relativization applies and the label stays absolute — which is the honest answer, because the file genuinely is not in the tree the memo ships. The tool already canonicalizes on both sides for its own reasons, `resolve_key` for the key and `Session::for_path` before asking git for the root, so this rule adds a comparison rather than a new mechanism.
## The decision, per artifact

Three artifacts ship together and they should be held to three different promises. A **rendered memo** guarantees that every tool-generated extent label naming a file inside the worktree its observation was taken against is spelled relative to that worktree root — and promises nothing about text an author typed, nor about a `proc:` command line. An **evidence ledger** inherits that guarantee for `predicate.extent[]`, and explicitly keeps `predicate.world[].root` absolute, because that field is the identity of a tree rather than a citation into one. A **snapshot** keeps every `key` absolute and canonical, because `key` is what the census predicate compares against `world_root`, and stores exactly the labels the memo renders. The whole thing is deliverable because label and key are already separate fields, the label is built at capture from a `world_root` that is already on the pending entry, and the two render sites print stored labels verbatim.

The evidence ledger deserves the arithmetic, because it is the noisiest artifact and the split is clean. Across the eight committed `.evidence.jsonl` files, 5621 machine-local path occurrences sit in `predicate.extent[]` — which `record` builds by cloning each fact extent entry's label, so a capture-time label change fixes all of them without touching `record` at all. Another 901 sit in `predicate.world[].root`, and those stay: a worktree root is what makes two observations comparable, and rewriting it would destroy the comparison the field exists for. Sixteen sit in a grader's free-text `note`. Nothing at all sits in `predicate.source`, `predicate.pin`, `world[].state` or the subject. So the ledger's promise is not "no machine paths" but "the citations are relative and the tree identity is absolute", which is a promise the code can keep.

The snapshot's promise is the narrowest of the three and the only one with a hard prohibition in it. Machine-local paths there are concentrated almost entirely in `facts.jsonl` — 448 of 448, 273 of 275 and 348 of 350 occurrences in the three memos measured, with `prose.jsonl`, `targets.jsonl`, `transplants.jsonl`, `counters.json`, `identity.json`, `pending.json` and `refusals.log` carrying none — so the label change reaches almost all of them. The prohibition is on `key`: `ExtentEntry::censuses` decides every `target` declaration by asking whether `self.key == self.world_root`, and `search_key` exists solely to make those two tool-captured spellings of one absolute directory agree. A relativized key would silently uncensus every modification target in the corpus. Keys stay absolute, and the contract says so out loud rather than leaving it as an implementation detail an optimiser might tidy away.

Two exclusions are stated in the contract rather than hidden in it, because a contract that overclaims is this ticket's own defect. Author-typed text is outside the guarantee: a claim proposition that names a path in prose stays exactly as written, and every memo in this corpus opens with one. `proc:` command lines are outside it too, for the stronger reason given below. The consequence is that a committed memo produced under the new contract will still contain machine-local paths, and the contract's job is to say precisely which ones and why — not to promise they are gone.

It is worth being precise about what is broken today, because the obvious guess is wrong. A memo, its evidence ledger and its snapshot copied alone into a fresh git repository at a different absolute path, with an empty state home and no workspaces at all, already check at exit 0 with no provenance drift. Citation ids resolve off-workspace. What does not survive the move is a reader's ability to *open* what a fact opened: against a clone of this repository at a different absolute path, the memo's absolute paths resolve to nothing, while stripping the worktree prefix from each memo's distinct in-repo paths resolves 32 of 35, 21 of 23 and 32 of 36 to files that exist there. A small residue does not resolve even relativized, and this design did not diagnose it — see the risks.

That is the whole benefit, and it is a portability benefit, not a privacy one. The distinction matters because privacy is the reading a reviewer will reach for on seeing `/Users/<someone>/` disappear, and it would be false. After this change a committed artifact still carries machine-local paths in author-typed claim propositions, in `proc:` command lines and the keys derived from them, in every extent `key`, and in `predicate.world[].root` — 901 occurrences of that last field alone across the eight committed evidence ledgers. Anyone wanting a privacy guarantee needs a different ticket and a different mechanism; this one must not be sold as delivering it.
## What happens to what is already committed

Nothing happens to them, and that is the design, not an omission. Extent and label are immutable per fact; the eight committed memos keep their absolute labels, keep their pins, and keep checking clean. A reader tells an old artifact from a new one by one added `#[serde(default)]` field on the extent entry, recording that this label was computed root-relative at capture. This is not a new idiom: `ExtentEntry` already carries four such fields — `world_root`, `kind`, `out_len` and `matcher` — each documented so that absence means *not recorded* rather than some default value. The fifth reads the same way.

Borrowing that idiom means inheriting its preconditions, and both are answerable here. The donor fields insist that absence never be read as a default — "never *zero*", "never *some default kind*" — and an unmarked label genuinely has no default reading: the CLI accepts a relative path and the pin tests exercise exactly that, while the MCP surface requires an absolute one, so the only true statement about an unmarked label is that it is spelled as whoever captured it typed it, with no resolvability guarantee. The donor fields also insist that absence disable a use and that the remedy be cheap. Here absence forbids reading a label as openable against the worktree root, and the remedy is a fresh `look` under the new build — the same remedy `kind` and `out_len` prescribe, for the same reason: the record cannot be repaired, only re-taken.
## The paths that cannot be relativized

Four categories stay absolute, and a committed document should say so where a reader will meet them. A `proc:` label and its key are the command line as it ran, and rewriting them would falsify the record of what executed. Every extent `key` stays absolute because the census predicate compares it against `world_root`. `predicate.world[].root` in an evidence ledger stays absolute because it is a tree's identity, not a citation into a tree. And author-typed text — every claim proposition, every note — is outside the mechanism entirely. The honest form of the doc comment `render_facts` should have carried is therefore not "a committed document should not carry `/Users/<someone>/...`" but a sentence naming these four and saying why each is deliberate.

A fifth case is degenerate rather than exempt, and an implementer will hit it first. `search_key` deliberately stores the worktree root's own spelling as the key of a whole-search record whenever the search root and the worktree root are the same directory — which is exactly the configuration the census predicate demands — so stripping the root from that key leaves nothing at all. The root needs an explicit spelling of its own, and the surrounding label carries more than a path: the `no-match` and `search` forms interpolate the search root together with an exclusion note that enumerates skipped paths in full. The work is contained: `PendingEntry` is named in source only by its definition, every construction site in `observe.rs`, and the fold in `mint`; `ExtentEntry` by `facts.rs`, `scope.rs`, `worldstate.rs`, `targets.rs` and `checks.rs` and no other file under `src/`; `render_facts` only within `compose.rs`, plus one mention in `ledger.rs`.
## Rejected alternatives

**Relativize at render.** Rejected because `snapshot::check` byte-compares a memo against a full re-render of its snapshot, so this reddens every committed memo on the commit that lands it — TET-43, detonated as a precondition of a ticket that was supposed to compose with it. **Store a separate relative field beside the absolute label.** Rejected for the same reason one step later: two fields means render must choose between them, which is a render change; and the pin hashes the label, so the hashed record would keep the absolute spelling and nothing would improve where it is actually fingerprinted.

**Relativize the key as well, for consistency.** Rejected: `ExtentEntry::censuses` decides every modification target by asking `self.key == self.world_root`, and a relative key answers that question wrongly and silently. **Strip the worktree prefix off the label string.** Rejected on a measured attack: a `look` through a symlink out of the repository, or one spelled with `..`, stores a label that textually begins with the repository root while naming a file outside it, and a prefix strip would mint a relative-looking citation to a file no reader of that repository has. Deriving the label from the canonicalized key instead makes those cases refuse themselves.

**Anchor at the memo's own directory.** Rejected on availability, not on merit: it is the better match for what a reader clones, but it does not exist when a label is built. It also does not currently differ from the worktree root for any committed memo. **Promise that a committed document carries no machine-local path.** Rejected as the ticket's own defect restated — it would be false of author-typed propositions and of `proc:` argv the moment it was written, exactly as the existing comment is false today. **Rewrite the artifacts already committed.** Rejected: it would drift all eight memos off a clean 0-of-8 baseline to buy retroactive tidiness in records that are immutable by design.
## Risks and unrun preconditions

Three things this design rests on that were established here, and three it did not run. Established: the drift baseline is 0 of 8 and any post-change measurement is against that, not against a pre-existing failure to hide behind; no code path or test recomputes or cross-compares a fact pin, so the pin discontinuity is free on this build; and off-workspace `check` already passes, so the gain is openability rather than checkability. Not run, because they need a build carrying the change: minting fixtures under it and reading which rows still carry a machine-local prefix; re-checking all eight committed memos under it to confirm the baseline is undisturbed; and re-measuring the repo-internal share on the first memo authored under it, which is the number that grades whether this earned its cost. The design rests on those three as unrun preconditions and says so rather than asserting their outcomes.

Four risks, in decreasing order of how likely they are to bite. A relative label is not self-describing and the rendered memo names no worktree root, so the author-typed pin claim is load-bearing until TET-43 makes room for the tool to state it. The anchor choice is safe only while no memo cites a repository other than the one it ships in — true of all eight today, and a cross-repository design would break the assumption silently rather than loudly. A small residue of in-repo paths does not resolve in a clone even when relativized, and this design did not diagnose it, so "82 percent become openable" is an upper bound rather than a delivered number. And the pin discontinuity is free only against today's readers: any future mechanism that compares a fact's pin across builds would meet a split corpus with no marker on the pin itself to explain it.

text: The whole-search label is the last case, and it is the one this design was most tempted to call degenerate and hand to the implementer. Measured, it is the opposite of a corner: it carries 113 of tet61's 218 machine-local path occurrences, 51 of tet47's 127 and 38 of tet56's 145 — more than the plain file labels in two of the three memos — and all of them name paths under the very worktree the memo ships in. Whatever gets chosen here decides more of TET-42's delivered benefit than the case the rest of this memo specifies, so it is decided here rather than deferred. Two things make it awkward. `search_key` deliberately stores the worktree root's own spelling as the key of a whole-search record whenever the search root and the worktree root are the same directory — exactly the configuration the census predicate demands — so stripping the root from that key leaves the empty string. And the label carries more than one path: the `no-match (ERE): {pattern} in {root} — {note}` and `search: {root} (…) — {note}` forms interpolate the search root *and* an exclusion note that enumerates every skipped memo path in full, listed rather than counted on purpose, so that two searches over different memo sets of the same size cannot pin identically. The decision: spell a search root that equals `world_root` as `.`, and put each path the exclusion note enumerates through the same key-derived rule as any other label — relative to `world_root` when it lies under it, absolute otherwise. The note's purpose survives, because distinct paths stay distinct under a common prefix strip and therefore still fingerprint differently. The work is contained: `PendingEntry` is named in source only by its definition, every construction site in `observe.rs`, and the fold in `mint`; `ExtentEntry` by `facts.rs`, `scope.rs`, `worldstate.rs`, `targets.rs` and `checks.rs` and no other file under `src/`; `render_facts` only within `compose.rs`, plus one mention in `ledger.rs`.

Promoted to a stated decision covering both the root spelling and the exclusion note's enumerated paths.

text: ## The paths that cannot be relativized, and the one that must be decided
why: The section now closes with a decision to relativize the whole-search label rather than a list of exemptions only; the heading was promising the wrong contents.

text: Relative to what? Two candidates deserve the question. The memo's own directory matches the distribution unit a reader actually clones, which is an honest argument for it. It loses on availability: a capture-time mechanism runs before `render --out` has been called, so the memo has no location yet to be relative to. `world_root` — the observation's own `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` — is already on the pending entry at the moment the label is built, resolved from the observed path rather than from any process's working directory. And the two choices do not diverge anywhere in the committed corpus: across every committed snapshot, each extent entry's world_root is either this repository or the degraded `no-git-worktree` marker, and no committed memo cites a fact taken against a repository other than the one it ships in. `world_root` wins on availability. It does not win for free, and the way it can fail is worth stating before the risks section rather than in it: `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` answers with the *innermost* repository, so a file checked in beneath the shipping worktree as its own repository — a submodule, a vendored checkout — is labelled relative to the inner root, not the outer one. Constructed and captured: an observation of `outer/vendor/sub/src/a.rs` in a nested repository derives the label `src/a.rs`, and `src/a.rs` exists in the outer worktree too, holding a different file — the label resolves, quietly, to the wrong thing, where the absolute label it replaces would have resolved to nothing at all. This repository has no submodules and no nested `.git` below its root, so nothing here reaches it today.
why: Answers the `qualifies` verdict on C16. The anchor's failure mode is not confined to a memo citing a repository elsewhere on the machine; a repository nested inside the shipping worktree produces a silently wrong label, and no reader would have read the old wording as covering that.

text: Four risks, in decreasing order of how likely they are to bite. A relative label is not self-describing and the rendered memo names no worktree root, so the author-typed pin claim is load-bearing until TET-43 makes room for the tool to state it. The anchor fails on a repository nested inside the shipping worktree — a submodule or a vendored checkout — as well as on one elsewhere on the machine, and the nested case is the worse of the two: `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` answers with the innermost repository, so the derived label can resolve against the outer worktree to a different file that exists there rather than failing loudly. Neither shape occurs in this repository today, and the design's answer is to name it rather than to defend against it. The delivered share is 38 to 52 percent of a memo's machine-local path occurrences before the whole-search decision and 85 to 95 after it; the 77-to-90-percent containment figure is an upper bound on what any worktree anchor could reach, not a delivered number, and a small residue of in-repo paths does not resolve in a clone even when relativized — this design did not diagnose that residue. And the pin discontinuity is free only against today's readers: any future mechanism that compares a fact's pin across builds would meet a split corpus with no marker on the pin itself to explain it.
why: Answers the `qualifies` verdicts on C16 and C12 where the risks paragraph carried them: the anchor risk said "a repository other than the one it ships in", which will not be read as covering a repository nested inside it, and the share sentence still presented 77-90 as the design's number.

text: All observations behind this memo were taken against the tetel worktree on branch `main` at commit `01b140c74882b17ccb157839cf205794a0aaaa49`. The tracked tree is clean; `git status --porcelain -b` is not empty, but the only entries it lists are three untracked ones, all of them this memo's own outputs — the memo, its `.evidence.jsonl` and its `.tetel/` snapshot. text: Three artifacts ship together and they should be held to three different promises, each stated at the width the mechanism actually delivers — plus one guarantee that is not per-artifact at all. A **rendered memo** guarantees that a tool-generated extent label is spelled relative to a repository root when three conditions hold together on the entry: its `world_root` resolved to a repository, its canonical key sits at or under that root, *and* the path as the caller spelled it lies under that same root. The third condition looks redundant and is not; the section on the forgery surface below shows the ordinary symlink that satisfies the first two and defeats the guarantee without it. Within that guarantee fall plain single-file labels and — by the decision below rather than by an implementer's discretion — a whole-search label's root and the in-repo paths its exclusion note enumerates. It promises nothing about text an author wrote, which means claim propositions *and* fact notes, the latter rendering in the Facts table's own Note column; nothing about a `proc:` command line; and nothing about an entry whose world marker degraded to `no-git-worktree`, which stays absolute even when the file is physically inside the shipping checkout; the committed corpus already contains one such entry, under this worktree's own `.git`. An **evidence ledger** inherits that guarantee for `predicate.extent[]` and explicitly keeps `predicate.world[].root` absolute, because that field is the identity of a tree rather than a citation into one. A **snapshot** keeps every key that is a path absolute — because `key` is what the census predicate compares against `world_root` — and canonical except where `search_key` deliberately adopts the world marker's `--show-toplevel` spelling for a whole-search root; it stores exactly the labels the memo renders. That clause is about path keys and nothing else: a `run` entry's key is `cmdline.clone()`, the command line itself, and `resolve_key` falls back infallibly to the caller's spelling when canonicalization fails on a path that exists. The fourth promise is the document's, not any single artifact's. Clause one is a per-entry rule, and a per-entry rule cannot see the failure where every entry is relativized correctly against its own root and the roots are not all the same tree; so the contract also requires `check` to report, out of `worldstate::tree_report`, the distinct roots a memo's relative labels are anchored to. That is a change to what `check` prints, not to what `render` writes, so no committed memo moves. The rest is deliverable because label and key are already separate fields, the label is built at capture from a `world_root` and a caller spelling both already on the pending entry, and both of the sites that render a label — the Facts table and the transplants section's donor extent line — print the stored string verbatim.

text: An extent entry carries two spellings of the same observation and they have different jobs. The key is the canonical form of the observed path — `resolve_key` canonicalizes, and falls back to the caller's spelling when canonicalization fails on a path that exists, so the key is absolute in practice rather than by construction. The label is the path exactly as the caller spelled it, plus a line-range suffix, and is what a human reads. `mint` copies both across from the pending buffer field by field and computes neither, so the only place a label can be made repo-relative is where it is first written, in `observe.rs` — and the anchor such a rewrite would need is already sitting on the same pending entry, because `world_root` is resolved from the observed path at capture time. It is worth being honest with the implementer about the size of that edit: `look_path` alone writes the label in three arms of one `match`, the grep path writes its own whole-search, no-match and per-file labels, and the whole-search label gets a rule of its own further down. This is a small set of expressions in one file, not a one-liner.

text: Nothing happens to them, and that is the design, not an omission. Extent and label are immutable per fact; the eight committed memos keep their absolute labels, keep their pins, and keep checking clean. A reader tells an old artifact from a new one by one added `#[serde(default)]` field on the extent entry, recording that this label was computed root-relative at capture. This is not a new idiom, though the precedent is narrower than the field count suggests. `ExtentEntry` already carries five `#[serde(default)]` fields — `world_root`, `kind`, `pattern`, `out_len` and `matcher` — so the marker would be the sixth. But only three of them say what the marker needs to say: `kind`, `out_len` and `matcher` each document absence as *not recorded*, never *some default kind*, never *zero*, never *some default grammar*. `world_root` reads differently, giving its own empty value a positive meaning — a state resolved from the process's working directory and therefore comparable with nothing — and `pattern` documents a plain default. The marker belongs with the three, and the argument below borrows from those three.
why: C7 revised: five default fields not four, and the "not recorded, never X" idiom holds literally on only three of them. The precedent argument now rests on the fields that actually share it.

text: Borrowing that idiom means inheriting its preconditions, and both are answerable here. The donor fields insist that absence never be read as a default — "never *zero*", "never *some default kind*" — and an unmarked label genuinely has no default reading. The design's first draft argued this from asymmetry: the CLI accepts a relative path and the pin tests exercise exactly that, while MCP requires an absolute one. The second half is false. `fn resolved` in `mcp.rs` joins a relative path onto the server's own working directory instead of refusing it, and the `look` handler does not call it at all — it forwards the caller's path verbatim. MCP documents absoluteness and enforces nothing. That makes the precondition easier to meet, not harder: absence cannot be read as "absolute" even by appeal to the surface it came in on, and it plainly cannot be read as "relative", so the only true statement about an unmarked label is that it is spelled as whoever captured it typed it, with no resolvability guarantee. The donor fields also insist that absence disable a use and that the remedy be cheap. Here absence forbids reading a label as openable against the worktree root, and the remedy is a fresh `look` under the new build — the same remedy `kind` and `out_len` prescribe, for the same reason: the record cannot be repaired, only re-taken.
why: C26 revised on a false premise: MCP does not enforce absolute paths on `look`. Correcting it strengthens the conclusion, and the paragraph should say so rather than keep asserting the enforcement.

text: It is worth being precise about what is broken today, because the obvious guess is wrong. A memo, its evidence ledger and its snapshot copied alone into a fresh git repository at a different absolute path, with an empty state home and no workspaces at all, already check at exit 0 with no provenance drift. Citation ids resolve off-workspace. What does not survive the move is a reader's ability to *open* what a fact opened. Measuring that needs a rule, because "distinct in-repo path" is not self-defining and three independent readers counting without one got three different answers: a path token here is the worktree root, then `/`, then a maximal run of `[A-Za-z0-9._/*-]`, with a trailing sentence period trimmed, deduplicated per memo — so the bare root is never a token. Against a clone of this repository at a different absolute path the absolute forms resolve to nothing, while stripping the root resolves 32 of 35 tokens for tet61, 22 of 23 for tet47 and 33 of 36 for tet56. The residue is five items in all and none of them is a relativization failure: `.idea`, `target` and `target/release/tetel` are git-ignored, `.git/COMMIT_EDITMSG` is git's own internal file, and `docs/design/tet*.md` is a literal glob off a command line and not a path at all.
why: C23 revised: the counting rule is now stated (its absence is why three graders got three numerators), the counts re-derived under it, and the residue diagnosed rather than deferred to the risks section.

text: The case for doing anything at all rests on a measurement, and it has to be the right measurement, counted under a rule that is stated. Counting one occurrence per literal `/Users/` or `/Volumes/` substring, the three memos carry 218, 127 and 145. How many of those are "inside the repository the memo ships in" depends on a second rule: requiring the root to be followed by a separator gives 195, 98 and 119 — 90, 77 and 82 percent — while counting the bare root too gives 218, 120 and 145, or 100, 94 and 100. Neither is an upper bound on what a worktree anchor can reach, and the first draft's claim that it was is refuted by this memo's own whole-search decision, which converts bare roots to `.` and so lands on 206 and 99 against a supposed ceiling of 195 and 98. What both figures share is that they classify by text alone, irrespective of whether the entry carrying an occurrence has a `world_root` that resolved, a key under that root, a caller spelling under the same root, or an exemption. Reclassified by this design's own rule, the mechanism converts 93 of tet61's 218, 48 of tet47's 127 and 75 of tet56's 145: 38 to 52 percent. That is the number the decision has to be made on, and the gap is not made of paths outside the worktree. Three parts of it are exclusions this design itself writes — `proc:` labels, the one entry whose world marker degraded, and above all the whole-search label, the largest single carrier in two of the three memos. The fourth part is not an exclusion the design chose and no capture-time change reaches it: 5, 10 and 13 occurrences of author-written text, mostly fact notes rendering in the Facts table's Note column. Two occurrences in five is still not cosmetics: a path rewritten from `/Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel/src/facts.rs` to `src/facts.rs` is openable by the next reader who clones the repository, which the absolute form is not. But a memo should not spend a containment figure on a mechanism that delivers 38 to 52 percent. Deciding the whole-search label — which the contract does rather than leaving it to the implementer — takes the delivered share to 206 of 218, 99 of 127 and 113 of 145, and that is the number that makes this comfortably worth doing.
why: C12 and C28 both revised: the "upper bound" claim is falsified by this memo's own C27, the containment figures needed their counting rule stated, and the exclusions are four buckets rather than three — the fourth being author-written text, which is not a design choice.

text: That is the whole benefit, and it is a portability benefit, not a privacy one. The distinction matters because privacy is the reading a reviewer will reach for on seeing `/Users/<someone>/` disappear, and it would be false. After this change a committed artifact still carries machine-local paths in author-written text — claim propositions and fact notes, the notes alone accounting for 5, 9 and 9 occurrences in the three memos measured and 5, 10 and 13 once the out-of-table occurrences are added — in `proc:` command lines and the keys derived from them, in every extent `key`, and in `predicate.world[].root`, 901 occurrences of that last field alone across the eight committed evidence ledgers. Anyone wanting a privacy guarantee needs a different ticket and a different mechanism; this one must not be sold as delivering it.
why: C24 revised to name fact notes and their measured size; the paragraph said "author-typed claim propositions" only, which understates the residue it is arguing from.

text: Before the contract, one point about who is at fault, because it decides whether this is a documentation fix or a code change — and the first draft of this memo got it wrong in a way worth recording. It argued that an absolute label is structural: that MCP, through which every agent authors, requires every path-taking parameter to be absolute, so an author who wanted a relative label could not produce one. MCP documents that requirement and does not enforce it. `fn resolved` joins a relative path onto the server's own working directory rather than refusing it, and the `look` handler never calls `resolved` at all; it forwards the caller's spelling straight through. A relative label over MCP is producible, and one was produced. What survives of the argument is the part that matters: the label is the path as the caller spelled it, nothing anywhere derives it from a root, and so the false comment still describes a mechanism nobody built. What does not survive is the stronger claim that the absolute spelling was inevitable. It is a convention with no enforcement behind it — which is why the schema marker below cannot let absence mean "absolute".
why: C14 revised: the MCP premise is false and was demonstrated live. The paragraph asserted the structural impossibility, which the claim no longer carries.

text: Relative to what? Two candidates deserve the question. The memo's own directory matches the distribution unit a reader actually clones, which is an honest argument for it. It loses on availability: a capture-time mechanism runs before `render --out` has been called, so the memo has no location yet to be relative to. `world_root` — the observation's own `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` — is already on the pending entry at the moment the label is built, resolved from the observed path rather than from any process's working directory, and that resolution is itself the result of a measurement: attaching the process's directory to every observation made the marker move when a repository nobody had read changed, so the tool asks about the file it opened. The two candidates do not diverge anywhere in the committed corpus: across every committed snapshot, each extent entry's world_root is either this repository or the degraded `no-git-worktree` marker, and no committed memo cites a fact taken against a repository other than the one it ships in. `world_root` wins on availability. It does not win for free, and the ways it fails are worth stating before the risks section rather than in it, because there are three of them and they do not have the same answer. First, a repository elsewhere on the machine, observed directly. Second, a repository nested beneath the shipping worktree — a submodule, a vendored checkout — because `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` answers with the *innermost* repository: constructed and captured, an observation of `outer/vendor/sub/src/a.rs` derives the label `src/a.rs`, and `src/a.rs` exists in the outer worktree too, holding a different file. Third, and the most ordinary of the three, a plain symlink from inside the shipping worktree into a separate repository, because `Session::for_path` canonicalizes the containing directory before asking git — so `look outer/link/x.txt` is attributed to whatever tree `link` points into. The third is closed at capture, by the rule the next section derives. The first two are not, and they are what the check-time report on distinct anchoring roots exists to surface. This repository has no submodules and no nested `.git` below its root, so nothing here reaches any of them today.
why: C16 revised to enumerate three divergence shapes rather than two, adding the symlink route that round-2 grounding constructed, and to say which mechanism answers which — the capture-time condition or the check-time report.

text: That choice comes with a gap the design must own rather than paper over, and this round it stops being deferred. `src/facts.rs` is only openable if the reader knows which tree it is relative to, and no artifact *declares* that tree. `check` does print the root — nine lines of its output on tet61 contain it — but every one is an incidental mention inside a quoted extent on a note-outside-extent row, and whether such a row exists at all depends on whether that memo happens to have those findings. There is no row saying "this memo's facts were taken against this root". Beyond that there is only the standing human-owed sentence about working-tree states, which names no root, plus the snapshot's `facts.jsonl` and, by convention, the author-typed pin claim that opens every memo in this corpus. Making the *memo* state its root would be a render change and is therefore TET-43's. Making *`check`* state it is not: `snapshot::check` compares the memo's bytes against a re-render of its snapshot, and check's own printed rows are outside that comparison. So the contract takes it. `worldstate::tree_report` already walks every fact's extent entries collecting `world_root`, and it is called from exactly one place inside the check driver; teaching it to report the distinct roots a memo's relative labels are anchored to, and to name them, answers "relative to what" and "is it one tree" in the same row, at the cost of one function and no drift.
why: C17 narrowed to declare-versus-mention (check does name the root incidentally), and C29 added: the gap is now closed inside this ticket via `tree_report` rather than deferred to TET-43.

text: Deriving the label from the key rather than from the caller's string is half the answer, and the first draft of this design stopped there. Under a key-derived rule the two escapes above refuse themselves: the key is not under the repository root, no relativization applies, and the label stays absolute — the honest answer, because the file genuinely is not in the tree the memo ships. But it is only half, and the other half was found by attacking the rule rather than restating it. Change the escape's destination from a directory to *another repository* and the key-derived rule stops refusing. Captured on the release build: `outer` is a repository, `outer/link` is a committed symlink to a separate repository `otherrepo`, and `look outer/link/x.txt` mints key `.../otherrepo/x.txt` with `world_root` `.../otherrepo`, because `Session::for_path` canonicalizes the containing directory before asking git. The key is strictly under that entry's own world_root. So the rule strips and mints `x.txt` — not absolute, not a refusal — and `x.txt` resolves in `outer` to a file that exists there holding "OUTER x" against the observed "OTHER FILE". That is the exact failure this design exists to prevent, reached through the mechanism chosen to prevent it, by an ordinary symlink rather than anything exotic. The fix is not to abandon the key, which still defeats the textual strip, but to require the two derivations to agree: relativize only when the caller's own spelling also lies under the same `world_root` the key is being stripped against. Here it does not — `.../outer/link/x.txt` is not under `.../otherrepo` — so the label stays absolute. In the control, `look outer/README.md`, key, label and world_root all agree and the strip applies. Both operands are on the pending entry already, so this is a second comparison, not a second mechanism, and it costs nothing on any observation that never left the tree the caller was working in. What it does not close is the case where a caller simply observes a file in another repository directly: there all three conditions hold and the label is relativized correctly against a tree the memo never names. Capture time cannot see that, because capture time does not know which memo this fact will end up in. The check-time report on distinct anchoring roots is where that one is caught.
why: C19 revised in mechanism: the key-derived rule alone does not refuse the symlink-into-another-repository case, so the paragraph's central assertion was false. It now states the attack, the added caller-spelling condition, and honestly names what remains open and where it is caught.

text: Five categories stay absolute, and a committed document should say so where a reader will meet them. A `proc:` label and its key are the command line as it ran, and rewriting them would falsify the record of what executed — the key of a `run` entry is not a path at all. Every extent key that *is* a path stays absolute because the census predicate compares it against `world_root`. `predicate.world[].root` in an evidence ledger stays absolute because it is a tree's identity, not a citation into a tree. Author-written text stays absolute and is two things, not one: every claim proposition, and every fact note — the notes being the larger half, 5, 9 and 9 occurrences across the three memos measured, and the easier half to overlook, because a note does not read as prose and yet renders straight into the Facts table's own Note column. And a label whose entry's world marker degraded to `no-git-worktree` stays absolute even when the file is physically inside the shipping checkout, because the mechanism has no root to anchor against; tet61's snapshot already carries one, a `look` at this worktree's own `.git/COMMIT_EDITMSG`. Outside those conditions the label is left exactly as the caller spelled it, and the contract stops there rather than promising it is absolute — the next paragraph says why that promise is not one this ticket can keep. text: Three artifacts ship together and they should be held to three different promises, each stated at the width the mechanism actually delivers — plus one guarantee that is not per-artifact at all. A **rendered memo** guarantees that a tool-generated extent label is spelled relative to a repository root when three conditions hold together on the entry: its `world_root` resolved to a repository, its canonical key sits at or under that root, *and* the path as the caller spelled it lies under that same root. That last comparison needs a resolution rule, because for a caller who typed a relative path it has no truth value until one is given — and the rule has to be one a second reader cannot read the other way, which is why it is spelled out rather than gestured at, down to which working directory it means. An absolute spelling is the literal string the caller typed. A relative spelling is the process's *physical* working directory — `std::env::current_dir()`, the getcwd(3) the operating system reports, in which the kernel has already resolved every symlink — and that string concatenated with a single separator between them: nothing is collapsed, no symlink is followed, no filesystem call is made. The condition holds exactly when the resulting string carries the root followed by a separator as a literal prefix. Two choices are being made there and the next two paragraphs each defend one: concatenating rather than normalizing `..` away first, and physical rather than logical. The third condition itself looks redundant and is not; the section on the forgery surface below shows the ordinary symlink that satisfies the first two and defeats the guarantee without it — and also shows the variant of that symlink the condition does *not* catch, which is routed to the fourth promise rather than papered over. Outside those conditions the label is left exactly as the caller spelled it, and the contract stops there rather than promising it is absolute — the next paragraph says why that promise is not one this ticket can keep. Within the guarantee fall plain single-file labels and — by the decision below rather than by an implementer's discretion — a whole-search label's root and the in-repo paths its exclusion note enumerates. It promises nothing about text an author wrote, which means claim propositions *and* fact notes, the latter rendering in the Facts table's own Note column; nothing about a `proc:` command line; and nothing about an entry whose world marker degraded to `no-git-worktree`, which stays absolute even when the file is physically inside the shipping checkout; the committed corpus already contains one such entry, under this worktree's own `.git`. An **evidence ledger** inherits that guarantee for `predicate.extent[]` and explicitly keeps `predicate.world[].root` absolute, because that field is the identity of a tree rather than a citation into one. A **snapshot** keeps every key that is a path absolute — because `key` is what the census predicate compares against `world_root` — and canonical except where `search_key` deliberately adopts the world marker's `--show-toplevel` spelling for a whole-search root; it stores exactly the labels the memo renders. That clause is about path keys and nothing else: a `run` entry's key is `cmdline.clone()`, the command line itself, and `resolve_key` falls back infallibly to the caller's spelling when canonicalization fails on a path that exists. The fourth promise is the document's, not any single artifact's. Clause one is a per-entry rule, and a per-entry rule cannot see two document-level failures: every entry relativized correctly against its own root while the roots are not all the same tree — three shapes now, a repository observed directly, a repository nested beneath the shipping worktree, and a working directory that reached another repository through a symlink — and a label the otherwise branch left relative, which a rendered memo cannot tell from a root-relative one because the marker is a snapshot field and both render sites print the label verbatim. So the contract also requires `check` to report, out of `worldstate::tree_report`, the distinct roots a memo's relative labels are anchored to and any relative label carrying no marker. That is a change to what `check` prints, not to what `render` writes, so no committed memo moves. The rest is deliverable because label and key are already separate fields, the label is built at capture from a `world_root` and a caller spelling both already on the pending entry — the working directory being the one operand a relative spelling needs that is *not* there, and that a fresh `current_dir()` call has to fetch — and both of the sites that render a label, the Facts table and the transplants section's donor extent line, print the stored string verbatim.

text: That leaves the rule itself, and it has to be decided rather than described, because "resolve the caller's spelling against the working directory" has two readings which are not stylistic variants: they give opposite answers on cases this memo relies on. text: Condition three closes that escape when the symlink is in the path the caller spelled. No fourth condition rescues this, and the reason is worth stating plainly rather than leaving as an omission: the only working directory a capture-time mechanism can obtain is `std::env::current_dir()`, in which the kernel has already resolved the symlink away, and `src/observe.rs` does not even consult that today — the whole crate reads a working directory at exactly two sites. The one operand that would answer the question, the spelling of the directory the caller believed they were standing in, does not exist anywhere in the process. So the rule names the physical one, because it is the only one that exists and the logical one would be worse; and this case is routed to the fourth promise, the check-time report of distinct anchoring roots, alongside the nested repository. Routing it there is not equivalent to closing it, and it is a worse residue than the nested case it joins. A nested repository takes a submodule or a vendored checkout to construct; this takes a `cd` through a symlink. The label it produces is shape-identical to a sound one, so nothing in the rendered memo distinguishes them. And the report is a human-owed row rather than a failure: it says a memo's labels are anchored to more than one root without saying which label is wrong, and where every label in a memo is anchored to one and the same wrong tree it names that root and nothing looks anomalous at all.

It does not win for free, and the ways it fails are worth stating before the risks section rather than in it, because they do not all have the same answer. First, a repository elsewhere on the machine, observed directly. Second, a repository nested beneath the shipping worktree — a submodule, a vendored checkout — because `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` answers with the *innermost* repository: constructed and captured, an observation of `outer/vendor/sub/src/a.rs` derives the label `src/a.rs`, and `src/a.rs` exists in the outer worktree too, holding a different file. So one case of four is closed at capture, and three residues — a repository elsewhere, a nested repository, a symlinked working directory — are what the check-time report on distinct anchoring roots exists to surface. This repository has no submodules and no nested `.git` below its root, so nothing here reaches any of them today.

text: Deriving the label from the key rather than from the caller's string is half the answer, and the first draft of this design stopped there. text: Condition three closes that escape when the symlink is in the path the caller spelled. It does not close it when the symlink is in the working directory, and this is where the design stops rather than adds a fourth condition. Captured on the release build: `cd outer/link` — the same committed symlink, now walked rather than typed — and then `look x.txt` mints key and `world_root` in `otherrepo`, and a bare `x.txt` anchored to `otherrepo`. All three conditions hold, because the working directory the process reads is the resolved `<s>/otherrepo` and the concatenation reproduces the key exactly. The label minted is byte-identical to the one the control capture from inside `outer` mints, and it resolves in the shipping tree to "OUTER x" against the observed "OTHER FILE". Two earlier drafts of this paragraph said no fourth condition could rescue this, on the ground that the untraversed spelling of the directory the caller believed they were standing in exists nowhere in the process. That is false, and the correction matters more than the conclusion it supports. Re-derived in the same fixture: after a shell `cd <s>/outer/link`, an external child process inherits `PWD=<s>/outer/link` — precisely the untraversed spelling — while `getcwd()` reports `<s>/otherrepo`, and `realpath(PWD) == getcwd()` is True, so the spelling is not only present but checkable against the physical directory without trusting the shell. A guard that reads `PWD`, uses it only under that equality, and otherwise falls back to `getcwd()` refuses this capture, because `<s>/outer/link` does not lie under the answering root `<s>/otherrepo`, and accepts the control `cd <s>/outer` unchanged. Everything this memo already measured about `PWD` survives and is what the equality test exists for rather than an argument against the guard: with the `chdir` performed by the process rather than by a shell, `PWD` stayed at `/Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel` while `getcwd()` had moved, so the test fails and the guard falls back; under `env -i` `PWD` is absent altogether; and over MCP, `fn resolved`'s own doc says the server cannot know the caller's working directory. The rule names the physical working directory, the case is routed to the fourth promise — the check-time report of distinct anchoring roots, alongside the nested repository — and routing it there is not equivalent to closing it. It is a worse residue than the nested case it joins. A nested repository takes a submodule or a vendored checkout to construct; this takes a `cd` through a symlink. The label it produces is shape-identical to a sound one, so nothing in the rendered memo distinguishes them. text: Three artifacts ship together and they should be held to three different promises, each stated at the width the mechanism actually delivers — plus one guarantee that is not per-artifact at all. A **rendered memo** guarantees that a tool-generated extent label is spelled relative to a repository root when three conditions hold together on the entry: its `world_root` resolved to a repository, its canonical key sits at or under that root, *and* the path as the caller spelled it lies under that same root. That last comparison needs a resolution rule, because for a caller who typed a relative path it has no truth value until one is given — and the rule has to be one a second reader cannot read the other way, which is why it is spelled out rather than gestured at, down to which working directory it means. An absolute spelling is the literal string the caller typed. A relative spelling is the process's *physical* working directory — `std::env::current_dir()`, the getcwd(3) the operating system reports, in which the kernel has already resolved every symlink — and that string concatenated with a single separator between them: nothing is collapsed, no symlink is followed, no filesystem call is made. The condition holds exactly when the resulting string carries the root followed by a separator as a literal prefix. Two choices are being made there and each is defended, in a different place: concatenating rather than normalizing `..` away first, two paragraphs below, and physical rather than logical, in the section on the forgery surface and again in the rejected-alternatives list — where the logical reading is declined as a default and a `PWD`-reading guard is declined for a separate reason, neither of them impossibility. The third condition itself looks redundant and is not; the section on the forgery surface below shows the ordinary symlink that satisfies the first two and defeats the guarantee without it — and also shows the variant of that symlink the condition does *not* catch, which is routed to the fourth promise rather than papered over. Outside those conditions the label is left exactly as the caller spelled it, and the contract stops there rather than promising it is absolute — the next paragraph says why that promise is not one this ticket can keep. Within the guarantee fall plain single-file labels and — by the decision below rather than by an implementer's discretion — a whole-search label's root and the in-repo paths its exclusion note enumerates. It promises nothing about text an author wrote, which means claim propositions *and* fact notes, the latter rendering in the Facts table's own Note column; nothing about a `proc:` command line; and nothing about an entry whose world marker degraded to `no-git-worktree`, which stays absolute even when the file is physically inside the shipping checkout; the committed corpus already contains one such entry, under this worktree's own `.git`. An **evidence ledger** inherits that guarantee for `predicate.extent[]` and explicitly keeps `predicate.world[].root` absolute, because that field is the identity of a tree rather than a citation into one. A **snapshot** keeps every key that is a path absolute — because `key` is what the census predicate compares against `world_root` — and canonical except where `search_key` deliberately adopts the world marker's `--show-toplevel` spelling for a whole-search root; it stores exactly the labels the memo renders. That clause is about path keys and nothing else: a `run` entry's key is `cmdline.clone()`, the command line itself, and `resolve_key` falls back infallibly to the caller's spelling when canonicalization fails on a path that exists. The fourth promise is the document's, not any single artifact's. Clause one is a per-entry rule, and a per-entry rule cannot see two document-level failures: every entry relativized correctly against its own root while the roots are not all the same tree — three shapes now, a repository observed directly, a repository nested beneath the shipping worktree, and a working directory that reached another repository through a symlink — and a label the otherwise branch left relative, which a rendered memo cannot tell from a root-relative one because the marker is a snapshot field and both render sites print the label verbatim. So the contract also requires `check` to report, out of `worldstate::tree_report`, the distinct roots a memo's relative labels are anchored to and any relative label carrying no marker. That is a change to what `check` prints, not to what `render` writes, so no committed memo moves. The rest is deliverable because label and key are already separate fields, the label is built at capture from a `world_root` and a caller spelling both already on the pending entry — the working directory being the one operand a relative spelling needs that is *not* there, and that a fresh `current_dir()` call has to fetch — and both of the sites that render a label, the Facts table and the transplants section's donor extent line, print the stored string verbatim.

text: One point about who is at fault, because it decides whether this is a documentation fix or a code change — and the first draft of this memo got it wrong in a way worth recording. It argued that an absolute label is structural: that MCP, through which every agent authors, requires every path-taking parameter to be absolute, so an author who wanted a relative label could not produce one. MCP documents that requirement and does not enforce it. `fn resolved` joins a relative path onto the server's own working directory rather than refusing it, and the `look` handler never calls `resolved` at all; it forwards the caller's spelling straight through. A relative label over MCP is producible, and one was produced. What survives of the argument is the part that matters: the label is the path as the caller spelled it, nothing anywhere derives it from a root, and so the false comment still describes a mechanism nobody built. What does not survive is the stronger claim that the absolute spelling was inevitable. It is a convention with no enforcement behind it — which is why the schema marker below cannot let absence mean "absolute".

text: Relative to what? Two candidates deserve the question. The memo's own directory matches the distribution unit a reader actually clones, which is an honest argument for it. It loses on availability: a capture-time mechanism runs before `render --out` has been called, so the memo has no location yet to be relative to. `world_root` — the observation's own `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` — is already on the pending entry at the moment the label is built, resolved from the observed path rather than from any process's working directory, and that resolution is itself the result of a measurement: attaching the process's directory to every observation made the marker move when a repository nobody had read changed, so the tool asks about the file it opened. The two candidates do not diverge anywhere in the committed corpus: across every committed snapshot, each extent entry's world_root is either this repository or the degraded `no-git-worktree` marker, and no committed memo cites a fact taken against a repository other than the one it ships in. `world_root` wins on availability. It does not win for free, and the ways it fails are worth stating before the risks section rather than in it, because they do not all have the same answer. First, a repository elsewhere on the machine, observed directly. Second, a repository nested beneath the shipping worktree — a submodule, a vendored checkout — because `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` answers with the *innermost* repository: constructed and captured, an observation of `outer/vendor/sub/src/a.rs` derives the label `src/a.rs`, and `src/a.rs` exists in the outer worktree too, holding a different file. Third, and the most ordinary of them, a plain symlink from inside the shipping worktree into a separate repository, because `Session::for_path` canonicalizes the containing directory before asking git — so `look outer/link/x.txt` is attributed to whatever tree `link` points into. The third splits in two on the rule the next section derives, and only one half is closed: the symlink typed into the path is caught, the symlink walked into by the working directory is not, because the rule reads the physical working directory and the kernel has already resolved the symlink away in it. That second half is left open by choice rather than by necessity — a guard reading `PWD` under a validity test against `getcwd()` would refuse it on the CLI, and is declined in the rejected-alternatives list because `PWD` is not the caller's over MCP. So one case of four is closed at capture, and three residues — a repository elsewhere, a nested repository, a symlinked working directory — are what the check-time report on distinct anchoring roots exists to surface. This repository has no submodules and no nested `.git` below its root, so nothing here reaches any of them today.

text: That leaves the rule itself, and it has to be decided rather than described, because "resolve the caller's spelling against the working directory" has two readings which are not stylistic variants: they give opposite answers on cases this memo relies on. Collapse `..` textually first, and a `look ../otherrepo/x.txt` issued from *inside* the shipping repository resolves to exactly the entry's own key — so all three conditions hold, and the rule mints a bare `x.txt` anchored to the other repository, which resolves in the shipping tree to a different file that exists there, "OUTER x" against the observed "OTHER FILE". That is the failure the third condition was introduced to prevent, reached through the third condition. Concatenate without collapsing, and the same spelling resolves to `<s>/outer/../otherrepo/x.txt`, which does not carry the answering root as a literal prefix, so the entry is refused and the label is left as typed. This design takes the concatenating rule — but not, as an earlier draft argued, because it refuses strictly more. That claim is false, and the counterexample is as ordinary as the case it was meant to cover: with `<s>/c` a symlink pointing back *inside* the repository, `look ../c/f.txt` from `<s>/outer` mints a key under `<s>/outer` whose concatenated spelling `<s>/outer/../c/f.txt` does carry the root as a literal prefix and is accepted, while the collapsed `<s>/c/f.txt` does not and is refused. Each rule accepts entries the other refuses; neither refusal set contains the other, and no argument from conservatism is available. What decides it is which acceptances are the right ones, and the reason concatenation gets them right is the same reason condition three exists at all: it is a test of which tree the caller's own frame of reference was, and only the spelling the caller actually issued carries that. Concatenation preserves it, so it refuses the `..` that leaves the shipping tree for another repository — where the caller was standing in one tree and the answering root is another — and accepts the `..` that leaves and re-enters, where the frame of reference and the answering root are the same tree and the key-derived label `sub/f.txt` opens against that root to exactly the file observed. Collapsing discards the spelling and gets both of those backwards. That is two constructed witnesses and a reason, not a theorem, and it is stated as such. It is also worth saying what condition three is *not* redundant for, because an earlier draft got the boundary wrong: it does not merely catch `..`. Measured on the release build, from `<s>/outer` the spelling `link/x.txt` — relative, with no `..` at all — mints key `<s>/otherrepo/x.txt` while the concatenation is `<s>/outer/link/x.txt`, so condition two passes and condition three refuses. The boundary is narrower still, and it was got wrong a second time: condition three adds nothing over condition two only for a relative spelling carrying neither a `..` component nor a symlink component *and* issued from a working directory lying at or under the answering root. The concatenation stays under the getcwd, not under the root, and `<root>/` is a literal prefix of it only when the root is the getcwd itself or an ancestor of it — which is the configuration every witness of the earlier wording happened to be taken in, the working directory standing at a repository root. Re-derived independently on the release build: from a scratch directory in no repository, the `..`-free, symlink-free spellings `./outer/x.txt`, `OUTER/x.txt` and `./otherrepo/x.txt` each pass condition two and are refused by condition three, and so are `./vendor/v.txt` and `VENDOR/v.txt` issued from a repository root against a nested repository beneath it — the shape where `--show-toplevel` answers with the innermost root and puts that root strictly below the getcwd — while the controls `outer/x.txt`, `outer/./x.txt`, `outer//x.txt`, `vendor/v.txt` and `vendor//v.txt` all pass from the same directories, so the break is a `.` or case-varying component landing at or above the answering root rather than `.` or `//` as such. Refusing at all does cost delivered share in principle, so the cost is measured rather than waved at: across the eight committed snapshots all 489 non-`proc:` extent entries — 82, 13, 12, 95, 43, 58, 79 and 107, against the eight `.md` files `git ls-files docs/design` calls tracked — carry an absolute caller spelling and not one of them contains a `..` component, so no committed entry is classified differently by the two readings, and the delivered figures below — 93, 48 and 75 before the whole-search decision, 206, 99 and 113 after it — hold under either. An earlier draft put that population at 804, because the glob behind it matched nine snapshot directories rather than eight: a memo under authoring has its snapshot on disk and untracked, so a measurement that globs `docs/design/*.tetel/` while the memo is in flight silently counts the memo's own uncommitted evidence as part of the corpus it is describing. The excess is deliberately not restated here as a number, because it has none that stays true — that snapshot grows with every fact this memo mints, the corrections included, so any difference stated is falsified by the act of stating it. The 489 and its per-directory parts are what is stable. The choice is therefore free on today's corpus and load-bearing on tomorrow's.
